item.title: Why Some Partners Don't View Unfaithful Behavior as Cheating
item.description:
Infidelity

Why Some Partners Don't View Unfaithful Behavior as Cheating

Why dark personalities view infidelity differently.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Machiavellianism and primary psychopathy predict how distinct acts are perceived as infidelity.
  • Dark personalties prefer short-term relationships, and are often emotionally aloof.
  • Healthy relationships are characterized by trust and avoiding relational temptation.
Source: Image by Екатерина Гусева from Pixabay

Trust remains one of the most significant hallmarks of successful relationships. So, when it comes to defining infidelity, do you know it when you see it? Apparently, different types of personalities view cheating differently. Research explains.

Infidelity Is in the Eye of the Beholder

Gayle Brewer et al. (2023) examined different perceptions of infidelity in a piece aptly entitled “But It Wasn’t Really Cheating,” specifically examining the viewpoints and behaviors of individuals with Dark Triad traits.[i] They begin by recognizing the three Dark Triad traits as distinct but interrelated, sharing features of lack of empathy and self-centeredness. Within romantic relationships, they note that Dark Triad individuals prefer uncommitted, short-term pairings.

Regarding the distinctions between the categories, Brewer et al. define Machiavellianism as “a strategic, long-term approach to personal relationships,” endorsing manipulation and a willingness to exploit others, and narcissism as involving a sense of superiority and entitlement. Regarding psychopathy, they recognize its link with callousness and impulsiveness but distinguish between primary psychopathy (callousness) and secondary psychopathy (risk-taking and impulsivity). They also found that different dark personalities view infidelity differently.

Personality Is Perception

Brewer et al. recognized five categories of infidelity: online, fantasized, emotional, sexual, and hidden attachment. They found that the Dark Triad traits of Machiavellianism and primary psychopathy predicted how distinct acts were perceived as infidelity, controlling for personal experience and demographic factors. And they explained why.

Brewer et al. explain that people who score high on Machiavellianism were not only less likely to view fantasizing as infidelity, but also less concerned with fantasy if it does not hinder their strategic objectives, such as to obtain status or control. Regarding the decreased likelihood of viewing expressed emotion as infidelity, they note that Machiavellianism is associated with attachment avoidance, preferring emotional and psychological independence, and discomfort with intimacy. Having a partner who has become emotionally attached to others may decrease the pressure they personally feel to exhibit intimacy and emotional closeness, resulting in feeling less distressed by their partner’s behavior.

Regarding the finding that people high in primary psychopathy were more apt to view emotional expression and fantasy as infidelity, Brewer et al. note that primary psychopathy is linked with a higher level of emotional jealousy. Therefore, they note, this link may reflect a higher amount of infidelity sensitivity. They also note that primary psychopathy is associated with less empathy and perspective taking, which could make it hard for someone with these characteristics to understand a partner's motivation for engaging in certain behavior. They give the examples of someone using sexual fantasy to achieve sexual release or having emotional relationships with others for companionship, noting that people high in primary psychopathy would be unable to separate these behaviors from others that present a more direct threat to the relationship.

Brewer et al. also found that individuals high in primary psychopathy were less likely to characterize sexual acts or hidden attachment as infidelity, perhaps reflecting a higher proclivity to engage in sexual infidelity themselves, facilitating justification of their own behavior. Brewer et al. also note that primary psychopathy is linked with self-serving sexual deception, making sexual infidelity and hidden attachment seem more acceptable or desirable.

Seeking a Meeting of the Hearts and Minds

Couples seeking relational quality and permanence should agree on what types of behaviors constitute infidelity and avoid activities that involve extra-relational temptation. Fulfilling relationships are characterized by trust, truth and transparency rather than deception. Plan accordingly, and date responsibly.

item.title: What “The Invite” Reveals About Sexless Marriages
item.description:
Marriage

What “The Invite” Reveals About Sexless Marriages

"The Invite" is not really about group sex.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • "The Invite," Olivia Wilde's 2026 film, silently exposes loud truths about sexless marriages.
  • Couples often forget that what happens in the bedroom reflects what happens outside of it.
  • The film shows the lengths we will go to distract or deflect from the pain of disconnection.
  • The path back to sexual intimacy is through emotional intimacy.

There’s a moment in The Invite, the 2026 dramedy by Olivia Wilde, that you could easily miss. It’s buried in the pre-orgy hilarity of the plot, which is intentional; humor is often used to camouflage our discomfort with sex. Pina, the vivacious and astute sexologist played by Penelope Cruz, asks the couple played by Wilde snd Seth Rogen, with the sincere curiosity of a scientist, “How do you have sex with each other? You are so mean to each other.”

Under the facade, lies the honest, uncomfortable truth.

As a sexologist, I’ve sat with countless people stuck in this intimacy no-man’s-land and it truly is a heartbreaking place. Sexless marriages are particularly hard to navigate because it is a deeply lonely place. Being in one is a hard thing to share, because it reeks of rejection. “My partner no longer desires me” is not something you can bring even to your closest confidante.

How do you define “sexless”?

Sexless marriages are highly personal and therefore, difficult to define. There is a commonly applied standard of “less than 10 times a year," but who gets to decide? What makes a relationship "sexless" anyway?

Like many things in the world of sex and relationships, there is art and there is science to it. But the reality of sexless marriages is this: You decide if you’re in one. Typically, a sexless marriage is anchored less in how much sex you’re having and more in the desire discrepancy: You’re not having as much sex as you want.

Sexless marriages can be devastating to a relationship, fueling a build-up of guilt, dejection and resentment. And the longer it goes on, the wider the gap can be, making a sexless marriage a tough place for a relationship to end up in and an even tougher one to climb out of.

What do we know about sexless marriages?

Studies show that it’s typically men who want more sex in a marriage. Is this biologically or culturally driven, because women have been taught to be frugal with their sexual impulse? Through my years exploring this topic, I’ve heard from many women who said they were the ones who wanted more sex—and that they were shamed for it. The pain of sexless marriages is real, and it cuts in both directions.

Culture matters too, especially the role of women in society — though its impact on sex in marriage isn’t intuitive. In traditional, patriarchal cultures, women are taught that their sexual role is to please their husbands and to produce children. In societies where women are more empowered, they exercise their right to say "no". So it may look like there are fewer sexless marriages in more traditional cultures, but that may be a function of convention, not choice.

Time impacts intimacy in marriage, too. Research shows that sexual satisfaction in newlyweds typically declines after 4-5 years. Life gets in the way — jobs, kids, and the like (although there is science that shows how to keep the spark going). Poor physical health and aging can be predictors of sexless marriages as well.

The Gottman Institute identified the four horsemen of a decaying relationship: criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling. Pina put it in simpler terms: You’re too mean to have sex.

Relationship expert Esther Perel has said, “Sexuality is a coded language for our deepest emotional needs, our wounds, our fears, our aspirations, our longings.” If a relationship doesn’t create an environment of safety, trust, and respect, true sexual intimacy will not sustain.

Make-up sex is glamorized. Sure, occasionally, sex is a great way to break through the tension of a fight, but what happens in the bedroom is a reflection of what happens outside it.

How can you save a sexless marriage?

When I coach people in sexless marriages, there are five things I ask them to think about:

  • Blame. Are you assigning the responsibility for this chasm on your partner, overtly or covertly? Blame is a non-starter on the path to healing.
  • Reflection. When and how did things change? There’s usually a turning point. If you can retrace your steps, it can provide clues to where the reconciling needs to commence.
  • Accountability. What is your role in creating the distance? How will you own your part of bridging it?
  • Baby Steps. What small steps can you take daily to re-establish trust and intimacy in your relationship?
  • Expectations. What does this new relationship look like now? What needed to shift to get here?

The Invite highlights the harsh truth that we will do anything to hide, escape, or deflect from the discomfort of rejection. But when it comes to sexless marriages, ownership and accountability are key, as is knowing that relationships morph over time and need its participants to evolve with it.

Every couple in a sexless marriage is quietly issuing this invitation to one other, whether they know it or not: Come back to care first. The rest will follow.
